title: Choosing a model and API setup
notes: Weigh each step on quality, speed and cost; output tokens cost five times as much as input tokens.
Start with the most capable model, measure, then move simple high-volume steps to a cheaper model once tests show quality holds.

slides.title: Choosing a model and API setup
slides.sub: Weigh quality, speed and price, then look inside a request and its response
sentences: In Module 1 you made your first model call, using a model name you simply copied.
In this lesson you will learn to choose that model on purpose.
Then we will open up a request and a response, so nothing in that call is a mystery.

slides.title: One family, three sizes

note.text: Input is what you send; output is what the model writes. Output costs 5 times as much.

sentences: Most providers offer a family of models, from large and careful to small and quick.
Claude Opus is the most capable, the best choice for planning, using tools and hard cases.
It costs four dollars per million input tokens, and twenty dollars per million output tokens.
Sonnet is a strong all-rounder, a little faster, at half that price.
Haiku is the fastest and by far the cheapest, ten cents in and fifty cents out, and it is good at simple, clear tasks.
Input tokens are what you send, and output tokens are what the model writes back.
Output costs five times as much as input, so long replies cost more than long prompts.

slides.title: Three questions for every step

cards.title: Quality
flow: Can it do this step well?

cards.title: Speed
flow: A customer is in live chat

sentences: Choosing a model means weighing three things, separately for each step your agent takes.
First, quality: can this model do this step well, every time?
That matters most for planning, choosing tools and reading tricky policy, and you judge it by testing on real tickets.
Second, speed: how long can someone wait for the answer?
A customer in live chat notices a slow reply, while an overnight report does not care.
Third, cost: the price per token, times the tokens per call, times the calls per day.
One ticket costs a fraction of a cent, but thousands a day add up.

slides.title: Rule of thumb: start capable, then measure

note.text: Switch a step only when your tests show the cheaper model still gets it right.

sentences: So which model should Scout use? Here is a rule of thumb that works well.
Start with the most capable model while you build, so when something fails, you know it is your design and not the model's limits.
Then measure: run real tickets through it, and record quality, speed and cost.
Look for steps that are simple and happen a lot, like tagging every incoming email by intent.
Move those steps to a cheaper model such as Haiku, and keep the hard steps on the capable one.
For a short email, tagging costs roughly four tenths of a cent on Opus, and about one hundredth of a cent on Haiku.
But switch only when your tests show the cheaper model still gets it right.
A cheap wrong answer is not a saving.

slides.title: What you send
slides.lead: One call to client.messages.create carries four things: the model, a length limit, the rules and the conversation.

rows.out: a ceiling on the reply, not a target

aside.label: Key stays outside
aside.text: anthropic.Anthropic() reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from your environment. Never write the key in code.

sentences: Now let us open up a request, using the same call you made in Module 1.
You call the messages create method, and first you name the model that should answer.
Max tokens is a ceiling on how long the reply may be, and the model usually stops well before it.
The system prompt holds standing instructions, like Scout's role and rules, which you will write later in this module.
Messages is the conversation itself: a list of turns, each with a role, user or assistant, and its content.
Other providers, such as OpenAI, Google or an open model, use the same ideas with slightly different field names.
And the client reads your API key from the environment variable you set in Module 1, so the key never appears in your code.

slides.title: What comes back
slides.lead: The reply is an object, not a string. Its text sits inside a list of content blocks.

rows.out: a list of blocks: maybe thinking, then text

rows.code: next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
rows.out: the text block, whatever comes first
why it stopped: end_turn or max_tokens
tokens written; input_tokens sits beside it

aside.label: Cut off?
aside.text: A stop_reason of max_tokens means the reply hit your ceiling mid-sentence. Raise the limit or ask for less.

sentences: Now the response.
Its content is not a plain string but a list of blocks, because the model may think before it answers.
So we take the first block whose type is text, with one short line of Python.
You will use that line in almost every program in this course.
The stop reason tells you why the model stopped: it finished its turn, or it ran into your max tokens ceiling.
Usage counts the input and output tokens, which you multiply by the price to know what the call cost.
If the stop reason is max tokens, the reply was cut off, so raise the limit or ask for a shorter answer.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Weigh each step on quality, speed and cost
Output tokens cost five times as much as input tokens
Start capable, measure, then move simple high-volume steps down
Send model, max_tokens, system, messages; read the text block back

sentences: Let us pull it together.
Weigh every step of your agent on quality, speed and cost.
Remember that output tokens cost five times as much as input tokens.
Start with the capable model, measure, and only then move simple, high-volume steps to a cheaper one.
A request names the model, a max tokens ceiling, the system prompt and the messages, and the reply's text sits in a list of blocks.
Next, the most useful skill in this module: writing prompts the model gets right.

midQuiz.q: On Claude Opus 5.5, which costs more: a million input tokens or a million output tokens?
options: Output tokens, five times as much
midQuiz.explain: Opus costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, so output is five times the price.
midQuiz.hint: Each row of the price table has two numbers. Which one is bigger?

midQuiz.q: You are building Scout's first version. Which model should you start with?
options: The cheapest one, to keep costs down from day one
The most capable one, then move simple steps to a cheaper model once you can measure
A different model for each customer, to compare them
midQuiz.explain: Starting capable shows you what good looks like. Then tests tell you which simple steps a cheaper model can take over.
midQuiz.hint: You can't judge a cheaper model until you know what a good answer looks like.

endQuiz.q: Some of Scout's replies stop mid-sentence. What should you check first?
options: Whether the API key is set
Whether the model name is spelled correctly
endQuiz.explain: A stop_reason of max_tokens means the reply hit your ceiling and was cut off. Raise the limit or ask for a shorter reply.
endQuiz.hint: The response itself tells you why the model stopped.

endQuiz.q: Why take the text with next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text") instead of response.content[0].text?
options: The first block may be the model's thinking, not the text
response.content is a single string, not a list
endQuiz.explain: The content is a list of blocks and the model may think before answering, so you pick the block whose type is text.
endQuiz.hint: What kind of block can arrive before the answer?
